title: Multisigs are classified on two independent axes — potential impact and required response speed — with ties rounded up
content:
A.2.11.1.3.2.1.1.1.1 defines an Impact Assessment producing one of four levels — Low (<$100k), Medium ($100k–$1M), High ($1M–$10M), Critical (>$10M) — each also characterized by decision context (from "[m]inimal disruption, alternative paths exist" to "[p]rotocol-wide failure") and reputational damage. A.2.11.1.3.2.1.1.1.2 defines a separate Operational Assessment producing Routine (24–48 hours, "[f]ull verification protocols"), Time-Sensitive (2–12 hours, "[s]treamlined but thorough"), or Emergency (<2 hours, "[m]inimal delays, risk-appropriate").

Separating the axes is the substantive insight. Blast radius and urgency are independent properties, and collapsing them into one "criticality" score forces a false trade: a high-value multisig that is never urgent should carry maximum verification, while an emergency pause key with no financial exposure should be fast and lightly gated. Only a two-dimensional grid lets security requirements be strict on one axis and permissive on the other.

Both provisions carry the same tie-break: "[w]hen a Multisig falls between two classification levels, the higher security classification must be selected." Since the Multisig Administrator self-assesses and reports to Core GovOps (A.2.11.1.3.2.1.1.8), the round-up rule removes the discretion that self-classification would otherwise create at every boundary — the classifier cannot resolve their own borderline case in favour of less work.

Accountability is attached before use: A.2.11.1.3.1.1 requires each Multisig to have a designated Administrator "communicated to the Protocol Security Workstream Lead and Core GovOps prior to the Multisig's activation or operational use."
description: Impact is graded Low to Critical by exposure, decision context and reputation; Operational is graded Routine to Emergency by response window, and borderline cases must take the higher classification.
